{{Short description|New Zealand mathematician and statistician (born 1960)}}
{{Use New Zealand English|date=December 2024}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2024|cs1-dates=ly}}
[[File:RSNZ honours Christchurch 2025 251028 Research-124 Mike Steel (cropped).jpg |thumb|Steel in 2025]]
'''Michael Anthony Steel''' (born May 1960) is a New Zealand mathematician and statistician, a distinguished professor of mathematics and statistics <ref name="profile">[https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/engineering/contact-us/people/mike-steel.html profile], retrieved 4 May 2022.</ref> and the director of the Biomathematics Research Centre at the [[University of Canterbury]] in [[Christchurch]], New Zealand.<ref name="cv">[http://www.math.canterbury.ac.nz/~m.steel/files/misc/cv.pdf Curriculum vitae], retrieved 7 March 2012.</ref> He is known for his research on modelling and reconstructing [[evolutionary tree]]s.

==Biography==
Steel studied at the University of Canterbury, earning a bachelor's degree in 1982, a masters in 1983, and a degree in journalism in 1985. He then moved to [[Massey University]], where he received his Ph.D. in 1989, supervised by [[Michael Hendy]]<!-- Q90112740 --> and [[David Penny]].<ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Distributions on bicoloured evolutionary trees : a thesis presented in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in Mathematics at Massey University |url= https://mro.massey.ac.nz/handle/10179/4216?show=full |publisher=Massey University |date=1989 |language=en |degree=Doctoral |first=Michael |last=Steel}}</ref> He joined the Canterbury faculty in 1994.<ref name="cv"/>

==Awards and honours==
Steel won the Hamilton Memorial Prize of the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]] in 1994; this prize is given annually to a New Zealand mathematician for work done within five years of a Ph.D.<ref>[http://ifs.massey.ac.nz/mathnews/NZMS65/presrep.html President's Report 1994/1995] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090617085559/http://ifs.massey.ac.nz/mathnews/NZMS65/presrep.html |date=17 June 2009 }}, New Zealand Mathematical Society, retrieved 7 March 2012.</ref>

In 1999 he won the research award of the [[New Zealand Mathematical Society]] "for his fundamental contributions to the mathematical understanding of phylogeny, demonstrating a capacity for hard creative work in combinatorics and statistics and an excellent understanding of the biological implications of his results."<ref>[http://nzmathsoc.org.nz/?awards New Zealand Mathematical Society awards], retrieved 7 March 2012.</ref>

He became a fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand in 2003.<ref>[http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/academy/fellowship/current-fellows/?ma-steel Fellow biography], RSNZ, retrieved 7 March 2012.</ref>

In 2018, Steel was elected as a [[ISCB Fellow|Fellow]] of the [[International Society for Computational Biology]], for his outstanding contributions to the fields of [[computational biology]] and [[bioinformatics]].<ref name="iscb-fellow">{{cite web|title=ISCB Fellows|url=https://www.iscb.org/iscb-fellows|website=www.iscb.org|accessdate=14 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320114530/https://www.iscb.org/iscb-fellows|archive-date=20 March 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Selected publications==
* Lockhart, Peter J., Michael A. Steel, Michael D. Hendy, and David Penny. "Recovering evolutionary trees under a more realistic model of sequence evolution." Molecular biology and evolution 11, no. 4 (1994): 605–612.
* Esser, Christian, Nahal Ahmadinejad, Christian Wiegand, Carmen Rotte, Federico Sebastiani, Gabriel Gelius-Dietrich, Katrin Henze et al. "A genome phylogeny for mitochondria among α-proteobacteria and a predominantly eubacterial ancestry of yeast nuclear genes." Molecular Biology and Evolution 21, no. 9 (2004): 1643–1660.
* Erdős, Péter L., Michael A. Steel, László A. Székely, and Tandy J. Warnow. "A few logs suffice to build (almost) all trees (I)." Random Structures & Algorithms 14, no. 2 (1999): 153–184.
* Erdös, Péter L., Michael A. Steel, LászlóA Székely, and Tandy J. Warnow. "A few logs suffice to build (almost) all trees: part II." Theoretical Computer Science 221, no. 1-2 (1999): 77–118.
